questions.question: What is abstraction in Java and how is it achieved?
questions.title: Abstraction in Java Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Abstraction** is the OOP principle of hiding implementation details and exposing only what a caller needs — the *what*, not the *how*. In Java you achieve it with **interfaces** (100% abstract — a pure contract) and **abstract classes** (partial — a mix of abstract and concrete methods). It's a design *principle*, separate from the `abstract` keyword.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand abstraction as a design idea (depend on contracts) and know the two Java mechanisms that deliver it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing abstraction (a principle) with the abstract keyword, or thinking abstraction is the same as encapsulation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie it to everyday code: declaring List<String> instead of ArrayList<String> is abstraction — you can swap the implementation without touching callers.

sections.title: Abstraction in Java — Quick Overview
sections.content:
**Abstraction** means hiding *how* something works and showing only *what* it does. You use it daily without thinking — a TV remote's 'volume up' button hides the circuitry; an ATM hides the banking system behind a few buttons.

In Java you express abstraction with two tools: an **interface**, which is a pure contract (100% abstraction — just method signatures), and an **abstract class**, which can mix abstract methods (no body) with concrete ones (partial abstraction). Callers depend on the contract, not the concrete class behind it.

The distinction that catches freshers: abstraction is a *design principle*. The `abstract` keyword is just one way to support it — an `interface` achieves full abstraction without using `abstract` at all.

sections.title: Abstraction at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What it is|~hide how, show what|expose essentials|hide implementation|the 'what' not the 'how'
blue|Interface|~100% abstraction|pure contract|method signatures only|implement with implements
emerald|Abstract class|~partial abstraction|abstract + concrete methods|shared state allowed|extend with extends
violet|Everyday use|~program to the interface|List not ArrayList|swap impl freely|callers unaffected

sections.title: How Abstraction Works
sections.content:
You define a contract, code against it, and choose the concrete implementation separately.

- An **interface** lists *what* operations exist; implementing classes provide *how*.
- Callers reference the **interface type**, so any implementation can be substituted.
- An **abstract class** captures shared code while leaving the varying parts abstract.
- The result is loose coupling: swapping `ArrayList` for `LinkedList` (or a fake in tests) changes nothing for callers.

sections.title: Abstraction via an Interface
Coupled to a concrete class
sections.content:
```java
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); // pinned to ArrayList
// Switching to LinkedList means editing this declaration everywhere.
```

sections.title: Abstracted — depend on the contract
sections.content:
```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();   // depend on List
names = new LinkedList<>();                // swap freely, zero callers affected
```
*Programming to the interface (`List`) instead of the implementation (`ArrayList`) is abstraction in everyday code.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing principle and keyword**: abstraction is a design idea; `abstract` is just one mechanism — interfaces give full abstraction without it.
- **Mixing it up with encapsulation**: encapsulation hides *data*; abstraction hides *complexity/implementation*.
- **Declaring concrete types**: `ArrayList<String> x = ...` couples callers; declare `List<String>` instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstraction** = hide the *how*, expose the *what*.
- **Interface** = 100% abstraction (pure contract); **abstract class** = partial (abstract + concrete).
- It's a **design principle**, not the `abstract` keyword.
- Program to the interface: `List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()`.
- Loose coupling — swap implementations (or fakes in tests) without touching callers.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Abstraction is the principle of hiding how something works and exposing only what it does. You use it every day without realizing — a TV remote has a volume button and you don't know the circuit behind it, an ATM lets you withdraw cash without exposing the banking system. In Java there are two ways to express abstraction. An interface is pure abstraction, a hundred percent contract — it just lists method signatures and the implementing classes provide the bodies. An abstract class is partial abstraction, because it can mix abstract methods that have no body with concrete methods that do, and it can hold shared state. The key idea is that callers depend on the contract, not on the concrete class behind it. So if I have a Shape interface with an area method, I can have Circle and Rectangle implement it differently, and code that loops over a list of shapes calling area has no idea which shape it's dealing with. The everyday version of this is writing List of String equals new ArrayList, instead of ArrayList of String equals new ArrayList. By declaring the interface type, I can swap to a LinkedList tomorrow and no calling code changes. The thing freshers get wrong is confusing the principle with the keyword. Abstraction is a design principle; abstract is just one Java keyword that supports it. An interface delivers full abstraction without using the abstract keyword at all. And it's not the same as encapsulation — encapsulation hides data, abstraction hides complexity and implementation.

questions.question: What is an abstract class in Java and what are its characteristics?
questions.title: Abstract Class in Java — Characteristics and Usage
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract class** is a class declared with the `abstract` keyword that **cannot be instantiated** and is meant to be extended. It can mix **abstract methods** (no body, must be overridden) with **concrete methods**, hold **fields and constructors**, and have any access modifiers — making it ideal for sharing common code across related subclasses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the full feature set of an abstract class and how it differs from an interface.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an abstract class must have abstract methods, or that it can't have constructors/fields/concrete methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that abstract classes shine for shared state + partial implementation (template method pattern), where interfaces can't hold instance state.

sections.title: Abstract Class — Quick Overview
sections.content:
An **abstract class** is declared with `abstract` and **cannot be instantiated directly** — you must subclass it. Its purpose is to provide a partially built base: shared code plus 'holes' that subclasses fill in.

An abstract class can contain **abstract methods** (signature only, subclasses must implement), **concrete methods** (full bodies, inherited as-is), **instance fields**, **constructors** (called via `super()` from subclasses), and **static members**. Unlike an interface, it can hold mutable instance state.

A subtle but important fact: an abstract class does *not* need any abstract methods — marking the class `abstract` is enough to forbid instantiation.

sections.title: Abstract Class Features
sections.content:
amber|Cannot instantiate|~must be subclassed|new on it fails to compile|extend it instead|defines a base type
blue|Abstract methods|~no body|subclass must override|signature only|the 'holes' to fill
emerald|Concrete methods|~full body|inherited as-is|shared logic|template behavior
violet|State & constructors|~unlike interfaces|instance fields allowed|constructor via super()|holds shared data

sections.title: Abstract Class with Shared + Abstract Methods
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'It must have abstract methods'**: false — an `abstract` class with zero abstract methods is still legal and still can't be instantiated.
- **'It can't have constructors'**: it can, and subclasses call them via `super()` — they run during subclass construction.
- **Trying to instantiate it**: `new Employee(...)` is a compile error; instantiate a concrete subclass.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Declared with `abstract`; **cannot be instantiated** — must be extended.
- Can mix **abstract** and **concrete** methods, and hold **fields** and **constructors**.
- Constructors run via `super()` during subclass construction (they initialize shared state).
- Doesn't *require* any abstract methods — `abstract` on the class is enough.
- Best when subclasses share state + partial implementation (template method).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: An abstract class is a class you declare with the abstract keyword, and the defining characteristic is that you can't instantiate it directly — you have to subclass it. Its whole purpose is to be a partially built base class: it gives you some shared, finished code, plus some holes that the subclasses are required to fill in. So an abstract class can contain abstract methods, which have just a signature and no body and force subclasses to provide an implementation. But it can also contain fully concrete methods that subclasses inherit as-is, which is where the shared logic lives. On top of that, unlike an interface, an abstract class can have instance fields and a constructor. The constructor is interesting — you can't call it with new on the abstract class, but the subclass calls it through super, and it runs while the subclass object is being constructed, to initialize the shared state. A good concrete example is an Employee base class with a name field, a concrete getName, an abstract calculatePay that every employee type implements differently, and a concrete printPayslip that calls calculatePay — that last one is the template method pattern. A couple of things freshers get wrong: they think an abstract class must have at least one abstract method, but that's not true — marking the class abstract is enough to forbid instantiation even with no abstract methods. And they think abstract classes can't have constructors, but they can; you just reach them through super from the subclass. The rule of thumb is: reach for an abstract class when your subclasses share both state and partial implementation, because an interface can't hold instance state.

questions.question: Can you instantiate an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Can You Instantiate an Abstract Class in Java?
questions.direct_answer: **No** — you cannot instantiate an abstract class with `new`, because it may have unimplemented (abstract) methods and represents an incomplete type. You instantiate a **concrete subclass** instead. You *can*, however, create an **anonymous subclass** on the fly (`new AbstractType() { ... }`), which is really instantiating a hidden concrete subclass.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why instantiation is forbidden and recognize the anonymous-subclass exception that looks like instantiating an abstract class.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing the `new AbstractType() { ... }` syntax instantiates the abstract class itself, rather than an anonymous concrete subclass.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that abstract classes still have constructors that run via super() during subclass construction — having a constructor doesn't mean you can call new on it.

sections.title: Instantiating an Abstract Class — Quick Overview
sections.content:
You **cannot** write `new AbstractType()` — the compiler rejects it. An abstract class can declare methods without bodies, so an instance of it could have 'missing' behavior; Java forbids creating such an incomplete object.

Instead you instantiate a **concrete subclass** that implements every abstract method. There's one syntax that looks like an exception: `new AbstractType() { ... }`. This is an **anonymous class** — you're actually defining and instantiating a hidden concrete subclass inline, not the abstract class itself.

Also note: an abstract class *does* have a constructor, but it runs via `super()` during subclass construction — having a constructor doesn't let you call `new` on it directly.

sections.title: Why You Can't Instantiate It
sections.content:
amber|Forbidden|~new AbstractType() fails|may have abstract methods|incomplete object|compile error
blue|Use a subclass|~concrete and complete|implements all methods|new Subclass() works|the normal path
emerald|Anonymous class|~looks like an exception|new Type(){...}|hidden concrete subclass|not the abstract class
violet|Has a constructor|~but you can't call it directly|runs via super()|inits shared state|during subclass build

sections.title: What Compiles and What Doesn't
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `new Animal() { ... }` instantiates the abstract class**: it instantiates an anonymous *subclass* that supplies the missing methods.
- **'It has a constructor, so I can call new'**: the constructor only runs via `super()` during subclass creation.
- **Forgetting to implement every abstract method**: a subclass that misses one must itself be declared `abstract`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `new AbstractType()` is a **compile error** — the type may be incomplete.
- Instantiate a **concrete subclass** that implements all abstract methods.
- `new AbstractType() { ... }` is an **anonymous concrete subclass**, not the abstract class.
- Abstract classes have constructors, but they run via `super()` — you still can't `new` them.
- A subclass that leaves any method abstract must itself be `abstract`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: No, you can't instantiate an abstract class directly — if you write new and the abstract type's name, the compiler rejects it. The reason is that an abstract class is allowed to declare methods with no body, so if Java let you create an instance of it, you'd have an object with missing behavior. To prevent that incomplete object from ever existing, instantiation is simply forbidden. What you do instead is instantiate a concrete subclass that implements every abstract method. So if Animal is abstract with an abstract sound method, I can't say new Animal, but I can say new Dog, where Dog extends Animal and implements sound. Now there's one piece of syntax that trips people up and looks like an exception. You can write new Animal followed by curly braces with method implementations inside. That seems like you're instantiating the abstract class, but you're not — that's an anonymous class. Java is actually defining a brand new, hidden concrete subclass right there and instantiating that. It only compiles because you supplied the missing method bodies in the braces. The other subtlety is constructors. An abstract class can have a constructor, and freshers sometimes assume that means they can call new on it. But that constructor only ever runs through a super call when a subclass is being constructed — it's there to initialize the shared state, not to let you instantiate the abstract type. And if a subclass forgets to implement even one abstract method, that subclass itself has to be marked abstract.

questions.question: What are the rules for abstract methods in Java?
questions.title: Rules for Abstract Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract method** has a signature but **no body** (`abstract void run();`) and can only exist inside an **abstract class** or an **interface**. Any concrete subclass **must override and implement** every abstract method. Abstract methods **cannot** be `private`, `static`, or `final`, because each of those would make overriding impossible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the exact legality rules for abstract methods, especially the modifier combinations that are illegal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an abstract method can be private/static/final, or that you can put an abstract method in a regular (non-abstract) class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the why: each forbidden modifier (private, static, final) defeats overriding, which is the whole point of an abstract method.

sections.title: Rules for Abstract Methods — Quick Overview
sections.content:
An **abstract method** declares *what* without *how*: a return type, name, and parameters, ending in a semicolon with no `{ }` body. It can live only in an **abstract class** or an **interface**, never in a concrete class.

The contract is strict: the first concrete subclass **must** override and implement every abstract method, or it too must be declared `abstract`. And three modifiers are illegal on an abstract method — `private`, `static`, and `final` — because each one removes the ability to override, which is the entire reason the method is abstract.

sections.title: Abstract Method Rules
sections.content:
amber|No body|~signature + semicolon|abstract void run();|no curly braces|subclass supplies body
blue|Where allowed|~abstract class or interface|never in concrete class|that's a compile error|home of the contract
emerald|Must override|~first concrete subclass|implements every one|or stays abstract|enforces the contract
rose|Illegal modifiers|~these break overriding|not private|not static|not final

sections.title: Legal vs Illegal Abstract Methods
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Abstract method in a concrete class**: illegal — the class must be `abstract` too.
- **Marking it `private`/`static`/`final`**: all illegal because they make overriding impossible.
- **Giving it a body**: an abstract method must end in `;` — a body makes it concrete and the `abstract` keyword invalid.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Abstract method = signature + `;`, **no body**.
- Only allowed inside an **abstract class** or an **interface**.
- The first **concrete** subclass must implement all of them (else it stays `abstract`).
- Cannot be **private**, **static**, or **final** — each prevents overriding.
- Interface methods are implicitly `public abstract` (unless `default`/`static`/`private`).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: An abstract method is a method that has a signature — a return type, a name, and parameters — but no body. You end it with a semicolon instead of curly braces, and the idea is that it declares what should happen without saying how. There are a few firm rules. First, an abstract method can only live inside an abstract class or an interface. If you try to put one in a regular concrete class, that's a compile error — the class itself would have to be marked abstract. Second, the contract has to be honored: the first concrete subclass must override and implement every abstract method it inherits, otherwise that subclass also has to be declared abstract. Third, and this is the part interviewers like to probe, three modifiers are illegal on an abstract method: private, static, and final. The reason ties them all together — the whole point of an abstract method is that subclasses override it. A private method isn't visible to subclasses, so it can't be overridden. A static method belongs to the class, not the instance, so it isn't polymorphically overridden either. And final explicitly means this can never be overridden. Every one of those contradicts the purpose, so the compiler rejects them. One more detail worth mentioning: in an interface, methods are implicitly public and abstract, so you don't even have to write those keywords — unless it's a default, static, or private method, which were added in Java 8 and 9.

questions.question: What were the changes to interfaces in Java 8 and why were they added?
questions.title: Java 8 Interface Changes — Default and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Java 8 added **default methods** (`default` keyword — methods with a body in an interface) and **static methods** to interfaces. They were introduced so the JDK could add new methods (like `List.sort` or `Collection.stream`) to existing interfaces **without breaking the millions of classes** that already implemented them. Java 9 later added **private** interface methods for shared helper logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know what default/static interface methods are and the real backward-compatibility reason they were added.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking default methods turn interfaces into abstract classes, or not knowing why they exist (the Collection.stream() evolution problem).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the diamond rule: if two interfaces give conflicting default methods, the implementing class must override and can call InterfaceName.super.method().

sections.title: Java 8 Interface Changes — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Before Java 8, an interface could only hold abstract methods and constants. Java 8 added two big things: **default methods** — methods with an actual body, marked `default` — and **static methods** on interfaces.

They exist for one practical reason: **interface evolution**. The JDK wanted to add `stream()` to `Collection` and `sort()` to `List`. Adding an abstract method to an interface would break every existing implementer overnight. A **default method** ships a ready-made implementation, so old classes keep compiling and automatically gain the new behavior.

Java 9 followed up with **private** interface methods to let default methods share helper code without exposing it.

sections.title: What Java 8/9 Added to Interfaces
sections.content:
amber|default method|~method with a body|marked default|inherited implementation|override optional
blue|static method|~utility on the interface|Comparator.comparing(...)|called on the interface|not inherited
emerald|Why: evolution|~add methods safely|Collection.stream()|no implementers break|backward compatible
violet|diamond conflict|~two default methods clash|must override|call X.super.method()|resolves ambiguity

sections.title: Default and Static Methods in an Interface
The problem default methods solved
Default methods make evolution safe
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking interfaces became abstract classes**: interfaces still have **no instance state** — default methods can't use fields.
- **Ignoring the diamond rule**: two conflicting default methods force the class to override; resolve with `X.super.method()`.
- **Overusing default methods**: they're for evolution and small convenience, not for dumping business logic into interfaces.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Java 8 added **default** (body) and **static** methods to interfaces; Java 9 added **private** ones.
- Reason: **safely evolve** published interfaces (e.g. `Collection.stream()`) without breaking implementers.
- Default methods are inherited and **optional to override**; static methods are called on the interface.
- Interfaces still hold **no instance state**.
- Diamond conflict → implementing class must override, using `InterfaceName.super.method()` if needed.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Before Java 8, an interface could only contain abstract methods and constants — no implementations at all. Java 8 changed that by adding default methods and static methods to interfaces. A default method is a method right inside the interface that actually has a body, and you mark it with the default keyword. A static method is a utility method you call on the interface itself, like Comparator.comparing. The reason they were added is really important, and it's the answer interviewers are listening for: interface evolution. The JDK team wanted to add stream to the Collection interface and sort to the List interface. The problem is, if you add a normal abstract method to an interface that's already out in the world, every single class that implements that interface instantly fails to compile, because now it's missing a method. That would have broken millions of classes. A default method solves it because it ships a ready-made implementation. Old classes keep compiling, and they automatically inherit the new behavior, but they can still override it if they want something custom. Java 9 then added private methods to interfaces so that several default methods could share helper logic without exposing it publicly. A couple of nuances I'd mention. Interfaces still can't hold instance state — a default method can't read fields, because there are none. And there's the diamond situation: if a class implements two interfaces that both define the same default method, the compiler can't choose, so the class must override it, and inside that override it can pick one explicitly by writing the interface name dot super dot the method.

questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java and how does it relate to abstraction?
questions.title: Functional Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **functional interface** is an interface with **exactly one abstract method** (the SAM — Single Abstract Method). It's the target type for **lambdas** and **method references**, which is why it powers Java's functional style. You mark it with `@FunctionalInterface` to let the compiler enforce the one-method rule. `Runnable`, `Comparator`, and `Function` are examples.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a functional interface is the abstraction a lambda implements, and the 'exactly one abstract method' rule.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface is required for lambdas, or that default/static methods count toward the single-abstract-method limit.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a lambda is just a concise implementation of that one abstract method — the functional interface is the contract that makes lambdas type-safe.

sections.title: Functional Interface — Quick Overview
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is an interface with **exactly one abstract method** — often called the **SAM** (Single Abstract Method). That single method is what a **lambda** or **method reference** implements, so functional interfaces are the bridge that makes Java's functional features type-safe.

You can annotate it with `@FunctionalInterface`; that's optional but recommended, because the compiler will then reject the interface if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method. **Default**, **static**, and **private** methods don't count toward the limit — only abstract methods do.

The `java.util.function` package ships common ones: `Function`, `Predicate`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`, plus older ones like `Runnable` and `Comparator`.

sections.title: Defining and Using a Functional Interface
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `@FunctionalInterface` is mandatory**: any interface with one abstract method works with lambdas; the annotation just adds a compile-time guard.
- **Counting default/static methods**: only **abstract** methods count toward the SAM rule.
- **Adding a second abstract method**: it stops being functional, and existing lambdas no longer compile.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Functional interface = **exactly one abstract method** (SAM).
- It's the **target type** for lambdas and method references.
- `@FunctionalInterface` is optional but makes the compiler enforce the rule.
- **Default/static/private** methods don't count toward the single-method limit.
- Common built-ins: `Function`, `Predicate`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`, `Runnable`, `Comparator`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A functional interface is just an interface that has exactly one abstract method. People call that the SAM, the single abstract method. The reason it matters is that this single method is what a lambda implements. When I write a lambda like a comma b arrow a plus b, the compiler needs to know what type that lambda is, and a functional interface provides exactly that contract — the lambda is a concise implementation of its one abstract method. So functional interfaces are really the bridge that makes lambdas and method references type-safe in Java. You can put the FunctionalInterface annotation on it. That annotation is optional — any interface with one abstract method already works with lambdas — but it's good practice because it tells the compiler to enforce the rule. If someone later adds a second abstract method, the interface won't compile, and you find out immediately instead of discovering that all your lambdas suddenly broke. An important detail is what counts toward that one-method limit: only abstract methods count. You can add as many default, static, or private methods as you like and the interface is still functional, which is exactly how Comparator stays a functional interface despite having lots of default and static helpers. Java ships a whole package, java.util.function, with the common ones — Function takes a value and returns another, Predicate returns a boolean, Consumer takes a value and returns nothing, Supplier produces a value — and older ones like Runnable and Comparator are functional interfaces too. So when an interviewer asks how this relates to abstraction: the functional interface is the abstraction, the contract, and the lambda is a lightweight implementation of it.
